title: Young Flute Player
altText: A young person plays a flute, shown close up against a dark background. Warm light falls on the face while the rest of the scene stays in shadow.

source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page text (title, year, medium, collection, public-domain statement)

context: An oil painting by Judith Leyster, a Dutch painter, made around 1630. The source page tags it with Music and Instruments. Leyster was one of the few women who worked as a professional painter in the Dutch Republic in the 1600s.

descriptions.k: A young person plays a flute. Can you see the flute? Look at the face. Light shines on it. The back is dark. What tune do you think is playing?
descriptions.g12: Judith Leyster painted this young flute player a long time ago. The face is bright and the background is dark. The player seems to be busy making music. What sound do you imagine, and what in the picture helps you hear it?
descriptions.g35: Judith Leyster painted Young Flute Player around 1630 in the Netherlands. The player is shown up close, with light on the face and darkness behind. Painters then often showed musicians to celebrate music and everyday life. Look at the face and the way the flute is held. What clues tell you how the player feels about the music?
descriptions.g68: In Young Flute Player (c. 1630), Leyster brings us very close to a single musician and lights the face against a dark background. Music was a popular subject in Dutch painting of the 1600s. Consider how the close view, the glow, and the shadows work together. What do they make you notice first, and what story do they suggest?
descriptions.g910: Leyster's Young Flute Player (c. 1630) isolates one musician through a tight view and strong contrast between lit face and dark ground. As a woman painter working in the Dutch Republic, she competed in a market that favored lively, informal subjects. How does the pairing of intimacy and theatrical light shape your reading of the figure's character and the painting's purpose?
descriptions.g1112: Young Flute Player (c. 1630) is often grouped with the lively, informal figure paintings of the Dutch Republic, and its tight framing and dramatic light invite comparison with the wider Northern tradition of contrasted lighting. Leyster, a rare woman professional painter of her time, makes performance feel immediate. How might the painting be read as a portrait, a genre scene, or a study of music, and what does each reading emphasize?

k.daily: What music do you think the player is making? Tell us a sound.
k.emotion: How does the player seem to feel? Show us with your face.
k.observation: Find the flute. Where is it, and what is the player doing with it?
k.analysis: What part of the picture do you look at first? Why?
k.line: Trace the shape of the flute with your finger in the air. Is it straight or curvy?
k.shape: What round shapes can you find on the player's face?
k.color: Which colors do you see in the light parts? Which colors do you see in the dark parts?
k.texture: Does the player's hair look smooth or messy? How can you tell?
k.space: Is the player close to you or far away? How do you know?
k.light: Where does the light shine brightest? Where is it hidden in shadow?
k.meaning: Why might a painter choose to paint someone playing music?
k.culture: What instruments do you know from your home or neighborhood?
k.technique: Leyster used oil paint. How might paint make light look warm?
k.personal: If you could play any instrument, which one would it be? Why?
k.critical: What would you add to the dark background if you could?

g12.analysis: Why does your eye go to the face before the dark background?
g12.line: Follow the flute with your finger. Which direction does it point, and where does it lead your eye?
g12.shape: Which shapes repeat in the head, cap, and shoulders?
g12.color: How does the warm color on the face stand out against the dark behind it?
g12.texture: How did Leyster show hair and cloth so they feel different from skin?
g12.space: How does the dark background make the player feel close to you?
g12.light: Where is the strongest light, and which parts fade into shadow?
g12.meaning: Why might people in the 1600s have liked paintings of music-makers?
g12.culture: How do people today share music in their communities, and how is it like or unlike this scene?
g12.technique: How do you think Leyster made the face glow in a dark picture?
g12.personal: If a friend played a tune for you, how would you want to remember the moment in a picture?
g12.critical: Which part of the painting would you change if you were the painter, and why?

g35.daily: What details of the flute player make this feel like a real moment instead of a posed picture?
g35.emotion: How does the glow on the face change the feeling of the scene?
g35.observation: Look closely at the hands, the flute, and the clothing. What small details did Leyster include?

g35.line: How does the line of the flute guide your eye across the picture?
g35.shape: How do the curves of the face and cap compare with the straight flute?
g35.color: How does warm color on the face stand against the dark, cool background?
g35.texture: How do the soft shapes of hair and cloth compare with the skin?
g35.space: Why does the tight close-up make you feel like you are standing near the player?
g35.light: How does the contrast of bright light and deep shadow bring the player forward?

g35.technique: What do you think Leyster had to do to make light look real with oil paint?
g35.personal: What song would you choose for this player, and which parts of the picture led you there?

g68.observation: Describe the face, cap, and flute. Which detail do you notice only after a second look?

g68.shape: Where do curved forms like the cap and face meet the straight form of the flute, and what is the effect?
g68.color: How do warm skin tones and the deep dark ground create contrast in this painting?
g68.texture: How does Leyster suggest different textures, like skin, hair, and fabric, with oil paint?
g68.space: How does the shallow dark space make the player seem near and the setting vague?
g68.light: How does the strong contrast between light and dark help create a dramatic moment?
g68.meaning: What might music-making have meant as a subject for painters in the Dutch Republic of the 1600s?
g68.culture: What does it tell you about 1600s Dutch society that a woman like Leyster worked as a professional painter?
g68.technique: How might Leyster have used light and shadow to model the face with oil paint?

g910.daily: How does Leyster's very tight framing of the Young Flute Player shape your sense of the player's personality?
g910.emotion: What emotional tone results from the lit face, the dark ground, and the concentrated pose?
g910.observation: Study how the instrument meets the face. What does that point of contact suggest about focus?
g910.analysis: How does the hierarchy of face, instrument, and dark ground direct your reading?
g910.line: How does the diagonal of the flute organize the composition and carry the eye?
g910.shape: How do rounded forms in the head and cap interact with the narrow, straight shape of the flute?
g910.color: How does the restricted palette of warm flesh tones and dark surroundings support the mood?
g910.texture: How do variations in brushwork distinguish skin, hair, and cloth in this oil painting?
g910.space: What does the compressed, shadowy space suggest about the scene's setting and its meaning?
g910.light: How does the drastic contrast between illuminated and shadowed areas function as drama and as a way of modeling form?
g910.meaning: How might Leyster use music as a subject to explore youth, play, or attention?
g910.culture: How does Leyster's career as a woman painter in the Dutch Republic enrich your reading of her subject choices?
g910.technique: What does the handling of light on the face reveal about Leyster's technical skill with oil paint?
g910.personal: What does the painting make you reconsider about how a moment of music can be pictured without sound?
g910.critical: How would you assess whether the painting succeeds as a portrait of a person rather than a type of musician?

g1112.daily: How does the close framing of the Young Flute Player negotiate between portrait, genre scene, and meditation on music?
g1112.emotion: How does the painting's emotional register emerge from sharp light contrasts and the player's absorbed pose?
g1112.observation: Examine the relationship between face, hands, and instrument. What does the arrangement suggest about performance as a subject?
g1112.analysis: How does the composition organize attention through diagonal placement and tonal contrast?
g1112.line: How does the strong diagonal of the flute structure the painting's rhythm and balance?
g1112.shape: How do curved facial forms and the slender, straight instrument create a productive tension?
g1112.color: How does a limited palette of warm flesh and dark ground heighten emotional and sensory impact?
g1112.texture: How do the varied surface effects of skin, hair, and fabric demonstrate oil painting's capacity for description?
g1112.space: How does the shallow, undefined space position the viewer in relation to the performer?
g1112.light: How does the dramatic contrast of lit and unlit areas relate to wider Northern traditions of contrasted lighting?
g1112.meaning: What competing meanings might scholars see in the figure of a young musician, and what evidence supports each?
g1112.culture: How does it matter to your interpretation that Leyster worked as a professional woman painter in a market dominated by men?
g1112.technique: What does the handling of light and dark reveal about Leyster's technical priorities and the demands of her market?
g1112.personal: How does the painting shape your sense of the gap between visual art and sound?
g1112.critical: What criteria would you use to decide whether the work is best valued as a record of its time or as an enduring study of absorption?

teacherNote.context: A c. 1630 oil painting by Judith Leyster showing a young flute player. The source page tags it Music and Instruments. Leyster is notable as a woman professional painter in the Dutch Republic.
directions: Play a short recording of a flute and ask students to draw what they imagine, then compare with Leyster's choices.
Ask students to describe how light directs attention, then sketch a classmate with a single lamp.
Discuss how women artists worked and were recognized in the 1600s, using only evidence students can support.
